summary:
Same-sex conduct has been a criminal offence in Gambia since the colonial era. The Criminal Code adopted in March 2025 removed the 2014 provision permitting life imprisonment for "aggravated homosexuality" and instead sets a five-year minimum sentence for "unnatural offences", defined in the statute as any homosexual act, with no stated maximum penalty; "gross indecency" carries three years. Regional reporting on the same criminal-law package confirms that the minimum sentence for homosexual acts was raised to five years.

The offence attaches to conduct rather than to declared identity, but gender expression is separately restricted. Section 167 of the Criminal Code, in force since 2013, forbids men to dress "as women" and is punishable by up to five years in jail or a fine of 50,000 Gambian dalasi. Citizens cannot change their legal gender, so a visitor whose documents do not match their presentation has no domestic route to correcting them.

Enforcement under the government of President Adama Barrow has been limited. The US State Department's 2021 human rights report recorded no prosecutions under the statute while documenting significant societal stigma and police harassment of LGBT persons, and the 2020 report recorded arrests together with societal discrimination. Outright International's country profile, updated March 2026, likewise assesses that the Barrow government has not typically enforced these provisions. The government has promised not to prosecute same-sex couples for consensual sexual acts, while stating that there are no plans for liberalisation of the homosexuality laws.

Enforcement under President Yahya Jammeh was broad and violent. On 15 May 2008 he gave homosexuals 24 hours to leave the country and ordered the Inspector General of Police and the director of the Gambia Immigration Department to conduct mass patrols to "weed bad elements in society", warning that any hotel, lodge or motel lodging such individuals would be closed down. In November 2014 state forces launched an investigation under the aggravated homosexuality law producing at least eight arrests, including at least four adult men, a 17-year-old boy and nine women; detainees were held at the National Intelligence Agency headquarters in Banjul and were allegedly tortured to compel confessions.

Other documented arrests concern foreign nationals and gender non-conformity. In June 2008 two Spanish men in their 50s, alleged to be gay, were arrested and detained at Kotu police station after taxi drivers reported them and were released reportedly after their government intervened. On 10 April 2012 a court remanded 18 men, 16 Senegalese, one Gambian and one Nigerian, arrested at a bar in the Tourism Development Area for "indecent practice" after police said they were wearing women's clothes; all charges were dropped on 1 August 2012. On 23 December 2008 Frank Boers, a 79-year-old Dutch national, was arrested at Banjul International Airport in possession of pornography including nude photographs of himself and Gambian men, and was convicted of indecency and fined 100,000 dalasis in lieu of a two-year sentence.

Same-sex couples have no legal recognition in Gambia, and no law or regulation protects residents against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. The country also prohibits LGBTQ people from adopting children.

Healthcare carries a documented privacy risk. In 2023 there were reports of healthcare workers refusing to honour LGBTQ+ people's privacy, which has negatively affected HIV care for LGBTQ+ Gambians. The 2014 statute's mandatory life sentence for gay or lesbian people living with HIV was a direct barrier to testing and treatment; that provision was removed by the March 2025 Criminal Code.
tangentialFactors:
Freedom House rated The Gambia "Partly Free" with 50 out of 100 in Freedom in the World 2024, recording improved political freedoms under Barrow after 22 years of Jammeh's rule while listing severe discrimination against LGBT+ people among the ongoing concerns.

Human Rights Watch's report State of Fear, published in September 2015, documents arbitrary arrests, torture and killings in Gambia under Jammeh, including his anti-gay rhetoric and explicit threats against LGBT people. Those findings describe the enforcement climate of the previous regime rather than the present one, but they establish the pattern of state conduct that the current statutes sit on top of.

A 2021-2023 survey found that 93% of Gambians would dislike or strongly dislike having a homosexual neighbour. Children are raised within strict male and female gender norms, non-conformity to the heterosexual norm is treated as deviant and taboo, and the country's media promotes misinformation and harmful stereotypes toward LGBTQ+ people. Private hostility of this scale is the main source of risk that does not depend on official action.

No incidents of conversion therapy, and no surgeries on intersex children or non-consenting adults, were reported. The absence of reports is not evidence of absence in a country where no LGBTQ+ organisation exists to record them.
localsOnly:
No LGBTQ+ organisations exist in Gambia after 2016, because operating is considered too dangerous. There is therefore no domestic body to turn to for documentation, accompaniment or legal referral.

Healthcare workers were reported in 2023 to be refusing to honour LGBTQ+ people's privacy, with negative consequences for HIV care. Section 167 of the Criminal Code continues to expose gender-non-conforming men to up to five years' imprisonment or a 50,000-dalasi fine.

The Barrow government has promised not to prosecute same-sex couples for consensual sexual acts, but has stated that there are no plans to liberalise the homosexuality laws. The criminal provisions therefore remain in force and available to prosecutors regardless of current practice.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no entry, visa or border-screening rules for trans visitors, and no information on how Gambian immigration officers treat passports with amended gender markers. That gap is unresolved rather than negative: nothing sourced indicates either a prohibition or a permissive practice.

No sourced data covers prosecutions, arrests or convictions under the March 2025 Criminal Code. The assessment that the Barrow government has not typically enforced the provisions rests on reporting through 2021 and a country profile updated March 2026, and the position after the 2025 re-enactment is not documented.

Whether section 167 has been used against anyone in recent years is not sourced. The provision is on the books with a stated penalty, but no enforcement instance appears in the inventory.

The absence of a stated maximum penalty for "unnatural offences" in the March 2025 statute is reported as drafted; whether this reflects deliberate drafting or an omission is unresolved.

Arrests of gay people are believed to have been common during Jammeh's presidency, but the inventory states that data is lacking, so no frequency can be given.

The UK Home Office country information package on sexual orientation and gender identity in Gambia, version 3.0 dated February 2023, is an asylum-risk, internal-relocation and certification assessment rather than a travel-safety assessment; its currency against the March 2025 Criminal Code is unresolved.
